arXiv:math/0606716v1 [math.AG] 28 Jun 2006

Reduction method for linear systems of plane curves with base fat points

Marcin Dumnicki
Abstract.

In the paper we develop a new method of proving non-speciality of a linear system with base fat points in general position. Using this method we show that the Hirschowitz-Harbourne Conjecture holds for systems with base points of equal multiplicity bounded by 4242.

Key words and phrases: 
Multivariate interpolation, linear systems, Hirschowitz–Harbourne conjecture.
1991 Mathematics Subject Classification
14H50; 13P10

1. Introduction

Let 𝕂\mathbb{K} be a field of characteristics zero, ℕ={0,1,2,…}\mathbb{N}=\{0,1,2,\dots\}, ℕ∗={1,2,…}\mathbb{N}^{\ast}=\{1,2,\dots\}, let ℝ\mathbb{R} denote the field of real numbers.

Definition 1.

Let D⊂ℕ2D\subset\mathbb{N}^{2} be finite (any such set will be called a diagram), let m1,…,mr∈ℕ∗m_{1},\dots,m_{r}\in\mathbb{N}^{*}, let p1,…,pr∈𝕂2p_{1},\dots,p_{r}\in\mathbb{K}^{2}. Define the 𝕂\mathbb{K}-vector space ℒD​(m1​p1,…,mr​pr)⊂𝕂⁡[X,Y]\mathcal{L}_{D}(m_{1}p_{1},\dots,m_{r}p_{r})\subset\mathbb{K}[X,Y]:

ℒD​(m1​p1CLOSE\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{D}(m_{1}p_{1} ,…,mrpr):=\displaystyle,\dots,m_{r}p_{r}):=
{\displaystyle\big\{ f=∑(β1,β2)∈Dc(β,β2)Xβ1Yβ2∣c(β1,β2)∈𝕂,∂α1+α2f∂Xα1​∂Yα2(pj)=0,\displaystyle f=\sum_{(\beta_{1},\beta_{2})\in D}c_{(\beta,\beta_{2})}X^{\beta_{1}}Y^{\beta_{2}}\mid c_{(\beta_{1},\beta_{2})}\in\mathbb{K},\frac{\partial^{\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}}f}{\partial X^{\alpha_{1}}\partial Y^{\alpha_{2}}}(p_{j})=0,
α1+α2<mj,j=1,…,r}.\displaystyle\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}<m_{j},j=1,\dots,r\big\}.

Define the dimension of the system of curves ℒD​(m1,…,mr)\mathcal{L}_{D}(m_{1},\dots,m_{r}) to be

dimℒD​(m1,…,mr):=min⁡dim𝕂{pj}j=1r,pj∈𝕂2⁡ℒD​(m1​p1,…,mr​pr)−1.\dim\mathcal{L}_{D}(m_{1},\dots,m_{r}):=\min_{\{p_{j}\}_{j=1}^{r},p_{j}\in\mathbb{K}^{2}}\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\mathcal{L}_{D}(m_{1}p_{1},\dots,m_{r}p_{r})-1.
Remark 2.

If points p1,…,prp_{1},\dots,p_{r} are in general position we have

dimℒD​(m1,…,mr)=dim𝕂ℒD​(m1​p1,…,mr​pr)−1.\dim\mathcal{L}_{D}(m_{1},\dots,m_{r})=\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\mathcal{L}_{D}(m_{1}p_{1},\dots,m_{r}p_{r})-1.

The system ℒD​(m1,…,mr)\mathcal{L}_{D}(m_{1},\dots,m_{r}) can be understood as a vector space of curves generated by monomials with exponents from DD having multiplicities at least m1,…,mrm_{1},\dots,m_{r} in rr general points.

Definition 3.

Let L=ℒD​(m1,…,mr)L=\mathcal{L}_{D}(m_{1},\dots,m_{r}) be a system of curves. Define the virtual dimension vdim\vdim of LL and the expected dimension edim\edim of LL

vdim⁡L\displaystyle\vdim L :=#​D−1−∑j=1r(mj+12),\displaystyle:=\#D-1-\sum_{j=1}^{r}\binom{m_{j}+1}{2},
edim⁡L\displaystyle\edim L :=max⁡{vdim⁡L,−1}.\displaystyle:=\max\{\vdim L,-1\}.

Intuitively, we should have dimL=edim⁡L\dim L=\edim L.

Definition 4.

We say that a system of curves LL is special if

dimL>edim⁡L.\dim L>\edim L.

Otherwise we say that LL is non-special.

Observe that by linear algebra we have always dimL≥edim⁡L\dim L\geq\edim L since multiplicity mm imposes (m+12)\binom{m+1}{2} conditions.

2. The Hirschowitz–Harbourne Conjecture

For systems of the form ℒd​(m1,…,mr):=ℒD​(m1,…,mr)\mathcal{L}_{d}(m_{1},\dots,m_{r}):=\mathcal{L}_{D}(m_{1},\dots,m_{r}), D={α∈ℕ2∣|α|≤d}D=\{\alpha\in\mathbb{N}^{2}\mid|\alpha|\leq d\} the well-known Hirschowitz–Harbourne Conjecture giving geometrical description of the speciality of a system was formulated in [9]. To formulate this conjecture consider the blowing-up π:ℙ~2→ℙ2\pi:\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\to\mathbb{P}^{2} in rr general points with exceptional divisors E1,…,ErE_{1},\dots,E_{r}.

Definition 5.

A curve C⊂ℙ2C\subset\mathbb{P}^{2} is said to be a −1-1-curve if it is irreducible and the self-intersection C~2\widetilde{C}^{2} of its proper transform C~⊂ℙ~2\widetilde{C}\subset\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}^{2} is equal to −1-1.

Conjecture 6 (Hirschowitz–Harbourne).

A system L=ℒd​(m1,…,mr)L=\mathcal{L}_{d}(m_{1},\dots,m_{r}) is special if and only if there exists a −1-1-curve C⊂ℙ2C\subset\mathbb{P}^{2} such that

L~.C~≤−2,\widetilde{L}.\widetilde{C}\leq-2,

where L~:=|d​π∗​(𝒪ℙ2​(1))−∑j=1rmj​Ej|\widetilde{L}:=|d\pi^{*}(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{2}}(1))-\sum_{j=1}^{r}m_{j}E_{j}|.

This conjecture was studied by many authors, we refer only to the recent results. For homogenous systems (m1=m2=m3=⋯=mr=:mm_{1}=m_{2}=m_{3}=\dots=m_{r}=:m), the above conjecture holds for m≤20m\leq 20 (see [4, 5]). In the general case the Conjecture holds for multiplicities bounded by 1111 (see [8]). Both these results were obtained with the help of computers.

For further information about the above conjecture see for example [3].

In this paper we develop a new method (called ’’diagram cutting‘‘) based on some properties of matrices assigned to systems of curves. This method allows providing easy proofs of non-speciality for large family of systems. Moreover, these proofs can often be found argorithmically with a computer program. Sometimes this needs a lot of computations, but then it can easily be checked ’’by hand‘‘.

As a result of the method we show that in order to check non-speciality of all homogeneous systems of bounded multiplicity mm it is enough to check a finite number of cases. This result was obtained in purely theoretical way.

The second result is Theorem 31 stating that Conjecture 6 holds for homogeneous multiplicities bounded by 4242. This result was obtained using a computer program.

3. Diagram cutting method

Before introducing the method we must establish the notation and say when a system is non-special in the language of matrices.

Definition 7.

Let j∈ℕ∗j\in\mathbb{N}^{*}, α∈ℕ2\alpha\in\mathbb{N}^{2}. Define the mapping

φj,α:𝕂⁡[X,Y]∋f↦∂|α|f∂Xα​(Pj,X,Pj,Y)∈𝕂⁡[Pj,X,Pj,Y],\varphi_{j,\alpha}:\mathbb{K}[X,Y]\ni f\mapsto\frac{\partial^{|\alpha|}f}{\partial X^{\alpha}}(P_{j,X},P_{j,Y})\in\mathbb{K}[P_{j,X},P_{j,Y}],

where Pj,X,Pj,YP_{j,X},P_{j,Y} are new indeterminates used instead of X,YX,Y.

We will use the following notation: ℳ⁡(n,k,R)\mathcal{M}(n,k;R) will denote the set of all matrices with nn rows, kk columns, and coefficients from RR (a ring or a field). For an M∈ℳ⁡(n,k,R)M\in\mathcal{M}(n,k;R) we write M[j,ℓ]M_{[j,\ell]} for the element of MM in the jj-th row and the ℓ\ell-th column.

Definition 8.

Let L=ℒD​(m1,…,mr)L=\mathcal{L}_{D}(m_{1},\dots,m_{r}) be a system of curves, let D={(α1,X,α1,Y),…,(αn,X,αn,Y)}D=\{(\alpha_{1,X},\alpha_{1,Y}),\dots,(\alpha_{n,X},\alpha_{n,Y})\}, αi,X,αi,Y∈ℕ\alpha_{i,X},\alpha_{i,Y}\in\mathbb{N} for i=1,…,ni=1,\dots,n. Let 𝒜={(j,β)∈ℕ×ℕ2∣|β|<mj,j=1,…,r}={𝔞1,…,𝔞c}\mathcal{A}=\{(j,\beta)\in\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}^{2}\mid|\beta|<m_{j},\;j=1,\dots,r\}=\{\mathfrak{a}_{1},\dots,\mathfrak{a}_{c}\}. Define the matrix M⁡(L)∈ℳ⁡(c,n,𝕂​[Pi,X,Pi,Y]i=1r)M(L)\in\mathcal{M}(c,n;\mathbb{K}[P_{i,X},P_{i,Y}]_{i=1}^{r}) as

M​(L)[j,k]:=φ𝔞j​(Xαk,X​Yαk,Y).M(L)_{[j,k]}:=\varphi_{\mathfrak{a}_{j}}(X^{\alpha_{k,X}}Y^{\alpha_{k,Y}}).

For given points p1=(p1,X,p1,Y),…,pr=(pr,X,pr,Y)∈𝕂2p_{1}=(p_{1,X},p_{1,Y}),\dots,p_{r}=(p_{r,X},p_{r,Y})\in\mathbb{K}^{2} we will use the natural evaluation mapping

νp1,…,pr:𝕂​[Pi,X,Pi,Y]i=1r∋f↦f|Pi,X↦pi,X,Pi,Y↦pi,Y∈𝕂.\nu_{p_{1},\dots,p_{r}}:\mathbb{K}[P_{i,X},P_{i,Y}]_{i=1}^{r}\ni f\mapsto f|_{P_{i,X}\mapsto p_{i,X},P_{i,Y}\mapsto p_{i,Y}}\in\mathbb{K}.
Proposition 9.

Let L=ℒD​(m1,…,mr)L=\mathcal{L}_{D}(m_{1},\dots,m_{r}) be a system of curves. Then dimL=#​D−rank⁡M⁡(L)−1\dim L=\#D-\rank M(L)-1.

Proof.

Let p1,…,pr∈𝕂2p_{1},\dots,p_{r}\in\mathbb{K}^{2} be points in general position. Consider the linear mapping

Φ:{f=∑(αX,αY)∈Dc(αX,αY)XαXYαY}∋f↦(νp1,…,pr∘φ𝔞j(f))j=1c∈𝕂c.\Phi:\big\{f=\sum_{(\alpha_{X},\alpha_{Y})\in D}c_{(\alpha_{X},\alpha_{Y})}X^{\alpha_{X}}Y^{\alpha_{Y}}\big\}\ni f\mapsto(\nu_{p_{1},\dots,p_{r}}\circ\varphi_{\mathfrak{a}_{j}}(f))_{j=1}^{c}\in\mathbb{K}^{c}.

We have ℒD​(m1​p1,…,mr​pr)=ker⁡Φ\mathcal{L}_{D}(m_{1}p_{1},\dots,m_{r}p_{r})=\ker\Phi. Let MM denote the matrix of Φ\Phi in bases {(α1,X,α1,Y),…,(αn,X,αn,Y)}\{(\alpha_{1,X},\alpha_{1,Y}),\dots,(\alpha_{n,X},\alpha_{n,Y})\}, {𝔞1,…,𝔞c}\{\mathfrak{a}_{1},\dots,\mathfrak{a}_{c}\}. We have

νp1,…,pr​(M​(L)[j,k])=M[j,k],\nu_{p_{1},\dots,p_{r}}(M(L)_{[j,k]})=M_{[j,k]},

hence rank⁡M⁡(L)=rank⁡M\rank M(L)=\rank M (we use the facts that char⁡𝕂=0\charfield\mathbb{K}=0 and p1,…,prp_{1},\dots,p_{r} are in general position). Now we compute

dimL=n−rank⁡M−1=#​D−rank⁡M⁡(L)−1.\dim L=n-\rank M-1=\#D-\rank M(L)-1.

∎

Definition 10.

Define the bidegree bdeg:𝕂​[Pi,X,Pi,Y]i=1r→ℕ2\bdeg:\mathbb{K}[P_{i,X},P_{i,Y}]_{i=1}^{r}\to\mathbb{N}^{2} given by bdeg⁡(Pi,X):=(1,0),bdeg⁡(Pi,Y):=(0,1)\bdeg(P_{i,X}):=(1,0),\bdeg(P_{i,Y}):=(0,1) for i=1,…,ri=1,\dots,r.

Proposition 11.

Let ℒD​(m1,…,mr)\mathcal{L}_{D}(m_{1},\dots,m_{r}) be a system of curves. Let MM be a square submatrix of M⁡(L)M(L) of size s∈ℕ∗s\in\mathbb{N}^{*}. After a necessary renumbering of columns and rows we can assume that MM is given by columns (α1,X,α1,Y),…,(αs,X,αs,Y)(\alpha_{1,X},\alpha_{1,Y}),\dots,(\alpha_{s,X},\alpha_{s,Y}) and rows 𝔞1,…,𝔞s\mathfrak{a}_{1},\dots,\mathfrak{a}_{s}. Then detM\det M is a bihomogeneous (w.r.t. bdeg\bdeg) polynomial of bidegree (∑i=1sαi,X,∑i=1sαi,Y)−γ(\sum_{i=1}^{s}\alpha_{i,X},\sum_{i=1}^{s}\alpha_{i,Y})-\gamma, where γ∈ℕ2\gamma\in\mathbb{N}^{2} depends only on the choice of rows.

Proof.
detM=∑σ∈Sssgn⁡(σ)​M[1,σ⁡(1)]​…​M[s,σ⁡(s)].\det M=\sum_{\sigma\in S_{s}}\sgn(\sigma)M_{[1,\sigma(1)]}\dots M_{[s,\sigma(s)]}.

For M[j,k]≠0M_{[j,k]}\neq 0 we have bdeg⁡M[j,k]=(αk,X,αk,Y)−βj\bdeg M_{[j,k]}=(\alpha_{k,X},\alpha_{k,Y})-\beta_{j}, where 𝔞j=(ℓj,βj)\mathfrak{a}_{j}=(\ell_{j},\beta_{j}) for some ℓj∈ℕ\ell_{j}\in\mathbb{N}, βj∈ℕ2\beta_{j}\in\mathbb{N}^{2}. Hence

bdegM[1,σ⁡(1)]⋯M[s,σ⁡(s)]=(∑i=1sαi,X,∑i=1sαi,Y)−∑i=1sβi.\bdeg M_{[1,\sigma(1)]}\cdots M_{[s,\sigma(s)]}=\bigg(\sum_{i=1}^{s}\alpha_{i,X},\sum_{i=1}^{s}\alpha_{i,Y}\bigg)-\sum_{i=1}^{s}\beta_{i}.

We finish the proof by taking γ=∑i=1sβi\gamma=\sum_{i=1}^{s}\beta_{i}. ∎

Proposition 12.

Let m∈ℕ∗m\in\mathbb{N}^{*}, let D⊂ℕ2D\subset\mathbb{N}^{2}. Assume that #​D=(m+12)\#D=\binom{m+1}{2}. Then L=ℒD​(m)L=\mathcal{L}_{D}(m) is non-special if and only if DD do not lie on a curve of degree m−1m-1.

Proof.

From the previous proof we can see that detM⁡(L)=c⋅f\det M(L)=c\cdot f, where ff is a monomial, c∈𝕂c\in\mathbb{K}. Let D={(α1,X,α1,Y),…,(αn,X,αn,Y)}D=\{(\alpha_{1,X},\alpha_{1,Y}),\dots,(\alpha_{n,X},\alpha_{n,Y})\}. For β=(βX,βY)\beta=(\beta_{X},\beta_{Y}), |β|<m|\beta|<m we have

M​(L)[(1,β),j]=φ(1,β)​(Xαj,X​Yαj,Y)=∏k=1βX(αj,X−k+1)⋅∏k=1βY(αj,Y−k+1)⋅P1,Xαj,X−βX​P1,Yαj,Y−βY.M(L)_{[(1,\beta),j]}=\varphi_{(1,\beta)}(X^{\alpha_{j,X}}Y^{\alpha_{j,Y}})\\ =\prod_{k=1}^{\beta_{X}}(\alpha_{j,X}-k+1)\cdot\prod_{k=1}^{\beta_{Y}}(\alpha_{j,Y}-k+1)\cdot P_{1,X}^{\alpha_{j,X}-\beta_{X}}P_{1,Y}^{\alpha_{j,Y}-\beta_{Y}}.

Since we are only interested in the value of cc we would like to compute the determinant of M=M​(L)X↦1,Y↦1M=M(L)_{X\mapsto 1,Y\mapsto 1}. By a suitable sequence of row operations we can change MM into the following matrix M′M^{\prime}

M[(1,β),j]′=αj,XβX​αj,YβY,detM≠0⇔detM′≠0.M^{\prime}_{[(1,\beta),j]}=\alpha_{j,X}^{\beta_{X}}\alpha_{j,Y}^{\beta_{Y}},\qquad\det M\neq 0\iff\det M^{\prime}\neq 0.

Now detM′=0\det M^{\prime}=0 if and only if rows of M′M^{\prime} are linearly dependent, but this happens if and only if DD lies on a curve of degree m−1m-1. ∎

Now we can present the diagram cutting method and prove that it can be used to bound the dimension of a system of curves.

Theorem 13.

Let m1,…,mr,mr+1,…,mp∈ℕ∗m_{1},\dots,m_{r},m_{r+1},\dots,m_{p}\in\mathbb{N}^{*}, let D⊂ℕ2D\subset\mathbb{N}^{2} be a diagram, let F:ℕ2∋(α1,α2)↦r1​α1+r2​α2+r0∈ℝF:\mathbb{N}^{2}\ni(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2})\mapsto r_{1}\alpha_{1}+r_{2}\alpha_{2}+r_{0}\in\mathbb{R} be an affine function, r0,r1,r2∈ℝr_{0},r_{1},r_{2}\in\mathbb{R}. Let

D1\displaystyle D_{1} :={(α1,α2)∈D∣F⁡(α1,α2)<0},\displaystyle:=\{(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2})\in D\mid F(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2})<0\},
D2\displaystyle D_{2} :={(α1,α2)∈D∣F⁡(α1,α2)>0}.\displaystyle:=\{(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2})\in D\mid F(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2})>0\}.

If L2:=ℒD2​(mr+1,…,mp)L_{2}:=\mathcal{L}_{D_{2}}(m_{r+1},\dots,m_{p}) is non-special and vdim⁡L2=−1\vdim L_{2}=-1 then

dimℒD​(m1,…,mp)≤dimℒD1​(m1,…,mr).\dim\mathcal{L}_{D}(m_{1},\dots,m_{p})\leq\dim\mathcal{L}_{D_{1}}(m_{1},\dots,m_{r}).
Proof.

Put L1:=ℒD1​(m1,…,mr)L_{1}:=\mathcal{L}_{D_{1}}(m_{1},\dots,m_{r}). We can compute the dimension of a system L:=ℒD​(m1,…,mp)L:=\mathcal{L}_{D}(m_{1},\dots,m_{p}) as dimL=#​D−rank⁡M⁡(L)−1\dim L=\#D-\rank M(L)-1. As D=D1∪D2D=D_{1}\cup D_{2}, in an appropriate basis the matrix M⁡(L)M(L) is of the following form

M⁡(L)=[M⁡(L1)K1K2M⁡(L2)].M(L)=\left[\begin{array}[]{c|c}M(L_{1})&K_{1}\\ \hline\cr K_{2}&M(L_{2})\\ \end{array}\right].

Take a maximal non-zero minor M′M^{\prime} of M⁡(L1)M(L_{1}) and consider the following square submatrix of M⁡(L)M(L):

M=[M′K1′K2′M⁡(L2)],M=\left[\begin{array}[]{c|c}M^{\prime}&K_{1}^{\prime}\\ \hline\cr K_{2}^{\prime}&M(L_{2})\\ \end{array}\right],

where K1′K_{1}^{\prime} and K2′K_{2}^{\prime} are suitable submatrices of K1K_{1} and K2K_{2}. It suffices to show that detM≠0\det M\neq 0. The columns of M′M^{\prime} are indexed by elements from some D1′⊂D1D_{1}^{\prime}\subset D_{1} hence the columns of MM are indexed by D′:=D1′∪D2D^{\prime}:=D_{1}^{\prime}\cup D_{2}. Let U=[M′​K1′]U=[M^{\prime}\;K_{1}^{\prime}], L=[K2′​M​(L2)]L=[K_{2}^{\prime}\;M(L_{2})] be submatrices of MM, let

𝒞:={C⊂D′∣#​C=#​D2}.\mathcal{C}:=\{C\subset D^{\prime}\mid\#C=\#D_{2}\}.

For C∈𝒞C\in\mathcal{C} define LCL_{C} (respectively UCU_{C}) as the submatrix of LL (resp. UU) given by taking the columns indexed by elements of CC. Now we can compute

detM=∑C∈𝒞ϵ⁡(C)​detLC​detUD′∖C,\det M=\sum_{C\in\mathcal{C}}\epsilon(C)\det L_{C}\det U_{D^{\prime}\setminus C},

for ϵ⁡(C)=±1\epsilon(C)=\pm 1. Observe that detLC∈𝕂⁡[Pr+1,X,Pr+1,Y,…,Pp,X,Pp,Y]\det L_{C}\in\mathbb{K}[P_{r+1,X},P_{r+1,Y},\dots,P_{p,X},P_{p,Y}], detUD′∖C∈𝕂⁡[P1,X,P1,Y,…,Pr,X,Pr,Y]\det U_{D^{\prime}\setminus C}\in\mathbb{K}[P_{1,X},P_{1,Y},\dots,P_{r,X},P_{r,Y}] and consider detM\det M as a polynomial of indeterminates {Pℓ,X,Pℓ,Y}ℓ>r\{P_{\ell,X},P_{\ell,Y}\}_{\ell>r} over 𝕂⁡[{Pℓ,X,Pℓ,Y}ℓ≤r]\mathbb{K}[\{P_{\ell,X},P_{\ell,Y}\}_{\ell\leq r}]. We have

detM=±detM′detM(L2)+f.\det M=\pm\det M^{\prime}\det M(L_{2})+f.

Assume that detM=0\det M=0. As detM′≠0\det M^{\prime}\neq 0 and detM⁡(L2)≠0\det M(L_{2})\neq 0 from the assumptions, we must have another non-zero term g∈𝕂⁡[{Pℓ,X,Pℓ,Y}ℓ>r]g\in\mathbb{K}[\{P_{\ell,X},P_{\ell,Y}\}_{\ell>r}] appearing in ff such that bdeg⁡(g)=bdeg⁡(detM⁡(L2))\bdeg(g)=\bdeg(\det M(L_{2})). but from the definition of D2D_{2} it is possible only when C=D2C=D_{2}, contradiction. ∎

4. Reduction of homogeneous systems

We will use the following notation for a sequence of multiplicities:

Definition 14.

Let m1,…,mr∈ℕ∗m_{1},\dots,m_{r}\in\mathbb{N}^{*}, k1,…,kr∈ℕk_{1},\dots,k_{r}\in\mathbb{N}. Define

(m1×k1,…,mr×kr)=(m1,…,m1⏟k1,…,mr,…,mr⏟kr).(m_{1}^{\times k_{1}},\dots,m_{r}^{\times k_{r}})=(\underbrace{m_{1},\dots,m_{1}}_{k_{1}},\dots,\underbrace{m_{r},\dots,m_{r}}_{k_{r}}).

We will use diagrams of the following form:

Definition 15.

Let a1,…,an,u1,…,un∈ℕa_{1},\dots,a_{n},u_{1},\dots,u_{n}\in\mathbb{N}. Define

(a1↑u1,…,an↑un):=⋃i=1n{i−1}×{ui,…,ui+ai−1}⊂ℕ2.(a_{1}^{\uparrow u_{1}},\dots,a_{n}^{\uparrow u_{n}}):=\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}\{i-1\}\times\{u_{i},\dots,u_{i}+a_{i}-1\}\subset\mathbb{N}^{2}.

Definition 17.

Let ℤ\mathbb{Z} denote the set of all integers. We say that two diagrams D1D_{1}, D2D_{2} are equivalent (or D1D_{1} is equivalent to D2D_{2}) if there exists α∈ℤ2\alpha\in\mathbb{Z}^{2} such that D1=D2+αD_{1}=D_{2}+\alpha.

Remark 18.

Observe that diagram (0↑0,…,0↑0,a1↑u1,…,an↑un)(0^{\uparrow 0},\dots,0^{\uparrow 0},a_{1}^{\uparrow u_{1}},\dots,a_{n}^{\uparrow u_{n}}) is equivalent to (a1↑u1,…,an↑un)(a_{1}^{\uparrow u_{1}},\dots,a_{n}^{\uparrow u_{n}}) is equivalent to (a1↑u1+u,…,an↑un+u)(a_{1}^{\uparrow u_{1}+u},\dots,a_{n}^{\uparrow u_{n}+u}).

Proposition 19.

Let m1,…,mr∈ℕ∗m_{1},\dots,m_{r}\in\mathbb{N}^{*}, let D1D_{1}, D2D_{2} be diagrams. If D1D_{1} and D2D_{2} are equivalent, then dimℒD1​(m1,…,mr)=dimℒD2​(m1,…,mr)\dim\mathcal{L}_{D_{1}}(m_{1},\dots,m_{r})=\dim\mathcal{L}_{D_{2}}(m_{1},\dots,m_{r}).

Proof.

Let D1+(α1,α2)=D2D_{1}+(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2})=D_{2}, let p1,…,pr∈𝕂2p_{1},\dots,p_{r}\in\mathbb{K}^{2} be points in general position. The maps

ℒD1​(m1​p1,…,mr​pr)∋f\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{D_{1}}(m_{1}p_{1},\dots,m_{r}p_{r})\ni f ↦Xα1​Yα2​f∈ℒD2​(m1​p1,…,mr​pr),\displaystyle\mapsto X^{\alpha_{1}}Y^{\alpha_{2}}f\in\mathcal{L}_{D_{2}}(m_{1}p_{1},\dots,m_{r}p_{r}),
ℒD2​(m1​p1,…,mr​pr)∋f\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{D_{2}}(m_{1}p_{1},\dots,m_{r}p_{r})\ni f ↦X−α1​Y−α2​f∈ℒD1​(m1​p1,…,mr​pr)\displaystyle\mapsto X^{-\alpha_{1}}Y^{-\alpha_{2}}f\in\mathcal{L}_{D_{1}}(m_{1}p_{1},\dots,m_{r}p_{r})

are well-defined (we can assume that none of the coordinates of p1,…,prp_{1},\dots,p_{r} are zero), linear and inverse to each other. ∎

Lemma 20.

Let m∈ℕ∗m\in\mathbb{N}^{*}, D=(1↑m−1,2↑m−2,…,(m−1)↑1,m↑0)D=(1^{\uparrow m-1},2^{\uparrow m-2},\dots,(m-1)^{\uparrow 1},m^{\uparrow 0}). Then ℒD​(m)\mathcal{L}_{D}(m) is non-special and vdim⁡ℒD​(m)=−1\vdim\mathcal{L}_{D}(m)=-1.

Proof.

By Lemma 12 it is enough to show that DD (Fig. 3 shows an example for m=3m=3) do not lie on a curve CC of degree m−1m-1. Let Lj={(x,y)∈ℝ2∣x+y+j=0}L_{j}=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}\mid x+y+j=0\}, j=0,…,m−1j=0,\dots,m-1. Observe that #⁡(D∩Lj)=j+1\#(D\cap L_{j})=j+1 so by Bezout Theorem and induction we have ⋃j=0m−1Lj⊂C\bigcup_{j=0}^{m-1}L_{j}\subset C, a contradiction. ∎

Remark 21.

Observe that we can do the same for diagram (m↑0,(m−1)↑0,…,1↑0)(m^{\uparrow 0},(m-1)^{\uparrow 0},\dots,1^{\uparrow 0}).

Lemma 22.

Let m∈ℕ∗m\in\mathbb{N}^{*}, D=(m↑m,m↑m−1,…,m↑0)D=(m^{\uparrow m},m^{\uparrow m-1},\dots,m^{\uparrow 0}). Then ℒD​(m×2)\mathcal{L}_{D}(m^{\times 2}) is non-special and vdim⁡ℒD​(m×2)=−1\vdim\mathcal{L}_{D}(m^{\times 2})=-1.

Proof.

Let F=y−m+12F=y-m+\frac{1}{2}. Observe that D=D1∪D2D=D_{1}\cup D_{2} (Fig. 4 shows an example for m=3m=3), where

D1\displaystyle D_{1} :={p∈D∣F⁡(p)<0}=(0,1↑m−1,2↑m−2,…,m−1↑1,m↑0),\displaystyle:=\{p\in D\mid F(p)<0\}=(0,1^{\uparrow m-1},2^{\uparrow m-2},\dots,m-1^{\uparrow 1},m^{\uparrow 0}),
D2\displaystyle D_{2} :={p∈D∣F⁡(p)>0}=(m↑m,m−1↑m,…,1↑m).\displaystyle:=\{p\in D\mid F(p)>0\}=(m^{\uparrow m},m-1^{\uparrow m},\dots,1^{\uparrow m}).

The diagram D1D_{1} is equivalent to (1↑m−1,2↑m−2,…,(m−1)↑1,m↑0)(1^{\uparrow m-1},2^{\uparrow m-2},\dots,(m-1)^{\uparrow 1},m^{\uparrow 0}) hence from Lemma 20 the system ℒD1​(m)\mathcal{L}_{D_{1}}(m) is non-special. The diagram D2D_{2} is equivalent to (m↑0,(m−1)↑0,…,1↑0)(m^{\uparrow 0},(m-1)^{\uparrow 0},\dots,1^{\uparrow 0}) so ℒD2​(m)\mathcal{L}_{D_{2}}(m) is non-special. As #​D2=(m+12)\#D_{2}=\binom{m+1}{2}, we can use Theorem 13 to obtain non-speciality of ℒD​(m×2)\mathcal{L}_{D}(m^{\times 2}). ∎

Lemma 23.

Let m,k∈ℕ∗m,k\in\mathbb{N}^{*}, D=(m↑k−1,m↑k−2,…,m↑0)D=(m^{\uparrow k-1},m^{\uparrow k-2},\dots,m^{\uparrow 0}). If m+1|km+1|k then L=ℒD​(m×2​km+1)L=\mathcal{L}_{D}(m^{\times 2\frac{k}{m+1}}) is non-special and vdim⁡L=−1\vdim L=-1.

Proof.

We proceed by induction on kk. For k=m+1k=m+1 we use the previous Lemma. Let k>m+1k>m+1. Take F=x−(m+1)+12F=x-(m+1)+\frac{1}{2}. Observe that D=D1∪D2D=D_{1}\cup D_{2} (Fig. 5 shows an example for m=3m=3, k=12k=12), where

D1\displaystyle D_{1} :={p∈D∣F⁡(p)<0}=(m↑k−1,…,m↑k−1−m),\displaystyle:=\{p\in D\mid F(p)<0\}=(m^{\uparrow k-1},\dots,m^{\uparrow k-1-m}),
D2\displaystyle D_{2} :={p∈D∣F⁡(p)>0}=(0,…,0,m↑k−(m+1)−1,…,m↑0).\displaystyle:=\{p\in D\mid F(p)>0\}=(0,\dots,0,m^{\uparrow k-(m+1)-1},\dots,m^{\uparrow 0}).

The diagram D1D_{1} is equivalent to (m↑m,…,m↑0)(m^{\uparrow m},\dots,m^{\uparrow 0}), hence from Lemma 22 the system ℒD1​(m×2)\mathcal{L}_{D_{1}}(m^{\times 2}) is non-special. The diagram D2D_{2} is equivalent to (m↑k−(m+1)−1,…,m↑0)(m^{\uparrow k-(m+1)-1},\dots,m^{\uparrow 0}) and from the induction hypothesis we get that system ℒD2​(m×2​k−(m+1)m+1)\mathcal{L}_{D_{2}}(m^{\times 2\frac{k-(m+1)}{m+1}}) is non-special. Now, Theorem 13 allows us to finish the proof. ∎

Lemma 24.

Let m,k,h∈ℕ∗m,k,h\in\mathbb{N}^{*}, D=(h↑k−1,h↑k−2,…,h↑0)D=(h^{\uparrow k-1},h^{\uparrow k-2},\dots,h^{\uparrow 0}). If m+1|km+1|k and m|hm|h then L=ℒD​(m×2​k​hm⁡(m+1))L=\mathcal{L}_{D}(m^{\times 2\frac{kh}{m(m+1)}}) is non-special and vdim⁡L=−1\vdim L=-1.

Proof.

We proceed by induction on hh. If h=mh=m then the situation was treated in the previous Lemma. Let h>mh>m. Take F=y+x−(k−1+m)+12F=y+x-(k-1+m)+\frac{1}{2}. Observe that D=D1∪D2D=D_{1}\cup D_{2} (Fig. 6 shows an example for m=3m=3, k=12k=12, h=9h=9), where

D1\displaystyle D_{1} :={p∈D∣F⁡(p)<0}=(m↑k−1,m↑k−2,…,m↑0),\displaystyle:=\{p\in D\mid F(p)<0\}=(m^{\uparrow k-1},m^{\uparrow k-2},\dots,m^{\uparrow 0}),
D2\displaystyle D_{2} :={p∈D∣F⁡(p)>0}=((h−m)↑k−1+m,…,(h−m)↑m).\displaystyle:=\{p\in D\mid F(p)>0\}=((h-m)^{\uparrow k-1+m},\dots,(h-m)^{\uparrow m}).

According to Lemma 23 the system ℒD1​(m×2​km+1)\mathcal{L}_{D_{1}}(m^{\times 2\frac{k}{m+1}}) is non-special. The diagram D2D_{2} is equivalent to ((h−m)↑k−1,(h−m)↑k−2,…,(h−m)↑0)((h-m)^{\uparrow k-1},(h-m)^{\uparrow k-2},\dots,(h-m)^{\uparrow 0}) and by the induction hypothesis the system ℒD2​(m×2​k⁡(h−m)m⁡(m+1CLOSE)\mathcal{L}_{D_{2}}(m^{\times 2\frac{k(h-m)}{m(m+1}}) is non-special. Again we finish the proof by using Theorem 13. ∎

Definition 25.

Let m∈ℕ∗m\in\mathbb{N}^{*}, h=m⁡(m+1)h=m(m+1). Define the set (called the end of layer systems)

EoLS(m)={\displaystyle\EoLS(m)=\{ ℒD(m×2​k+h−1)∣\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{D}(m^{\times 2k+h-1})\mid
D=(h↑k−1,…,h↑0,(h−1)↑0,…,1↑0),k=1,…,m+1}.\displaystyle D=(h^{\uparrow k-1},\dots,h^{\uparrow 0},(h-1)^{\uparrow 0},\dots,1^{\uparrow 0}),k=1,\dots,m+1\}.

Observe that for every L∈EoLS⁡(m)L\in\EoLS(m) we have vdim⁡L=−1\vdim L=-1.

Lemma 26.

Let m,k∈ℕ∗m,k\in\mathbb{N}^{*}, h=m⁡(m+1)h=m(m+1), p=2​k+h−1p=2k+h-1, D=(h↑k−1,h↑k−2,…,h↑0,(h−1)↑0,…,1↑0)D=(h^{\uparrow k-1},h^{\uparrow k-2},\dots,h^{\uparrow 0},(h-1)^{\uparrow 0},\dots,1^{\uparrow 0}). If the set EoLS⁡(m)\EoLS(m) contains only non-special systems then the system L=ℒD​(m×p)L=\mathcal{L}_{D}(m^{\times p}) is non-special.

Proof.

Take k1,k2∈ℕk_{1},k_{2}\in\mathbb{N} such that k=k1​(m+1)+k2k=k_{1}(m+1)+k_{2}, 1≤k2≤m+11\leq k_{2}\leq m+1. Put F=x−k1​(m+1)+12F=x-k_{1}(m+1)+\frac{1}{2}. Observe that D=D1∪D2D=D_{1}\cup D_{2} (Fig. 7 shows an example for m=3m=3, k=11k=11), where

D1\displaystyle D_{1} :={p∈D∣F⁡(p)<0}=(h↑k−1,h↑k−2,…,h↑k2),\displaystyle:=\{p\in D\mid F(p)<0\}=(h^{\uparrow k-1},h^{\uparrow k-2},\dots,h^{\uparrow k_{2}}),
D2\displaystyle D_{2} :={p∈D∣F⁡(p)>0}=(h↑k2−1,…,h↑0,h−1↑0,…,1↑0).\displaystyle:=\{p\in D\mid F(p)>0\}=(h^{\uparrow k_{2}-1},\dots,h^{\uparrow 0},h-1^{\uparrow 0},\dots,1^{\uparrow 0}).

The diagram D1D_{1} is equivalent to the diagram (h↑k−k2−1,h↑k−k2−2,…,h↑0)(h^{\uparrow k-k_{2}-1},h^{\uparrow k-k_{2}-2},\dots,h^{\uparrow 0}) and since m+1|k−k2m+1|k-k_{2}, it follows from Lemma 24 that ℒD1​(m×2​(k−k2)​hm⁡(m+1))\mathcal{L}_{D_{1}}(m^{\times 2\frac{(k-k_{2})h}{m(m+1)}}) is non-special. The system ℒD2​(m×2​k2+h−1)∈EoLS⁡(m)\mathcal{L}_{D_{2}}(m^{\times 2k_{2}+h-1})\in\EoLS(m) and we can use Theorem 13 to complete the proof. ∎

Theorem 27.

Let m,dL∈ℕ∗m,d_{L}\in\mathbb{N}^{*}. Assume that for d=dL,…,dL+m⁡(m+1)d=d_{L},\dots,d_{L}+m(m+1) every system ℒd​(m×p)\mathcal{L}_{d}(m^{\times p}), p∈ℕp\in\mathbb{N}, is non-special. Moreover, assume that the set EoLS⁡(m)\EoLS(m) contains only non-special systems. Then for any d≥dL,p∈ℕd\geq d_{L},p\in\mathbb{N} the system ℒd​(m×p)\mathcal{L}_{d}(m^{\times p}) is non-special.

Proof.

We proceed by induction on dd. For dL≤d≤dL+m⁡(m+1)d_{L}\leq d\leq d_{L}+m(m+1) the proof is obvious. Take d>dL+m⁡(m+1)d>d_{L}+m(m+1). We want to show that the system ℒD​(m×p)\mathcal{L}_{D}(m^{\times p}) is non-special, where D=((d+1)↑0,…,1↑0)D=((d+1)^{\uparrow 0},\dots,1^{\uparrow 0}). Take h=m⁡(m+1)h=m(m+1), F=y+x−(d−h)+12F=y+x-(d-h)+\frac{1}{2}. Observe that D=D1∪D2D=D_{1}\cup D_{2} (Fig. 8 shows an example for m=3m=3, dL=3d_{L}=3, d=16d=16), where

D1\displaystyle D_{1} :={p∈D∣F⁡(p)<0}=(d+1−h↑0,…,1↑0),\displaystyle:=\{p\in D\mid F(p)<0\}=(d+1-h^{\uparrow 0},\dots,1^{\uparrow 0}),
D2\displaystyle D_{2} :={p∈D∣F⁡(p)>0}=(h↑d+1−h,…,h0,h−1↑0,…,1↑0).\displaystyle:=\{p\in D\mid F(p)>0\}=(h^{\uparrow d+1-h},\dots,h^{0},h-1^{\uparrow 0},\dots,1^{\uparrow 0}).

As d+1−h≥dLd+1-h\geq d_{L} we may use the induction hypothesis for the system ℒD1​(m×p−(2​d−h+3))\mathcal{L}_{D_{1}}(m^{\times p-(2d-h+3)}). By Lemma 26 the system ℒD2​(m×2​d−h+3)\mathcal{L}_{D_{2}}(m^{\times 2d-h+3}) is non-special. Again we finish the proof by using Theorem 13. ∎

Definition 28.

Let m,d0∈ℕ∗m,d_{0}\in\mathbb{N}^{*}. Put

S⁡(m,d0):=EoLS⁡(m)∪{ℒd(m×r)∣vdimℒd(m×r)≥−2m2,d0≤d≤d0+m(m+1),r∈ℕ∗}.S(m,d_{0}):=\EoLS(m)\cup\\ \{\mathcal{L}_{d}(m^{\times r})\mid\vdim\mathcal{L}_{d}(m^{\times r})\geq-2m^{2},d_{0}\leq d\leq d_{0}+m(m+1),r\in\mathbb{N}^{*}\}.
Theorem 29.

Let m,d0∈ℕm,d_{0}\in\mathbb{N}. If the set S⁡(m,d0)S(m,d_{0}) contains only non-special systems then every system ℒd​(m×r)\mathcal{L}_{d}(m^{\times r}) for d≥d0d\geq d_{0}, r∈ℕr\in\mathbb{N} is non-special.

Proof.

By Theorem 27 it suffices to show that every system ℒd​(m×r)\mathcal{L}_{d}(m^{\times r}), r∈ℕr\in\mathbb{N}, d=d0,…,d0+m⁡(m+1)d=d_{0},\dots,d_{0}+m(m+1), is non-special. Let L=ℒd​(m×r)L=\mathcal{L}_{d}(m^{\times r}). If vdim⁡L≥−2​m2\vdim L\geq-2m^{2} then LL is non-special by the assumptions. Let vdim⁡L<−2​m2\vdim L<-2m^{2}. From now on we use the notations and theory of reductions introduced in [7, 8]. We want to apply a sequence of rr weak mm-reductions to the diagram D={α∈ℕ2∣|α|≤d}D=\{\alpha\in\mathbb{N}^{2}\mid|\alpha|\leq d\} to end with the empty diagram,

D⟶m​ wD1⟶m​ wD2⟶m​ wD3⟶m​ w…⟶m​ w∅.D\stackrel{{\scriptstyle m\textrm{ w}}}{{\longrightarrow}}D_{1}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle m\textrm{ w}}}{{\longrightarrow}}D_{2}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle m\textrm{ w}}}{{\longrightarrow}}D_{3}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle m\textrm{ w}}}{{\longrightarrow}}\dots\stackrel{{\scriptstyle m\textrm{ w}}}{{\longrightarrow}}\varnothing.

Following the notations of [8] let us consider a diagram D=(a1,a2,…,an)D=(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{n}). Observe that the mm-reduction is not possible only if ai=ai+1<ma_{i}=a_{i+1}<m. As DD is the result of a sequence of weak mm-reductions this can only happen for i≤2​mi\leq 2m. While performing a mm-weak reduction we use at most mm additional points for each aia_{i}, i=1,…,2​mi=1,\dots,2m, and for each ii it is sufficient to do it only once. So we use at most 2​m22m^{2} additional points to reduce DD to the empty diagram, hence if vdim⁡L<−2​m2\vdim L<-2m^{2} then LL is non-special. ∎

5. Homogeneous systems with bounded multiplicity

Theorem 31.

The Hirschowitz-Harbourne Conjecture holds for homogeneous systems with multiplicities bounded by 4242.

Proof.

For m<20m<20 the result can be found in [5]. For m=20,…,42m=20,\dots,42 we choose d0​(m)=3​md_{0}(m)=3m. In order to check the conjecture we have to do the following:

  1. (1)

    Find all non-special systems among ℒd​(m×r)\mathcal{L}_{d}(m^{\times r}) for d≤d0​(m)d\leq d_{0}(m) (there are only finitely many of them). Next, for every such system we must show that it satisfies the Hirschowitz-Harbourne conjecture. This was done with the help of computer programs. By the proof of Theorem 29 the maximal size of matrix (for m=42m=42) can be 8128×116568128\times 11656, but in most cases the combination of reduction method and Cremona transformation gives an immediate answer.

  2. (2)

    For every system from the set S​(m,d0​(m))S(m,d_{0}(m)) we must prove its non-speciality.

As the set S​(m,d0​(m))S(m,d_{0}(m)) contains systems with big size of diagrams, this cannot be done without preparations. For a system L=ℒD​(m×r)∈EoLS⁡(m)L=\mathcal{L}_{D}(m^{\times r})\in\EoLS(m) we use reduction method described in [8] to reduce the problem to the question about non-speciality of L′=ℒD′​(m×5)L^{\prime}=\mathcal{L}_{D^{\prime}}(m^{\times 5}) for some diagram D′D^{\prime}. For m=42m=42 this forces us to compute the determinant of 4515×45154515\times 4515 matrix 4343 times — this can be done. For the rest of the systems from S​(m,d0​(m))S(m,d_{0}(m)) we use the following fact (see Proposition 28 in [8]).

Theorem 32.

Let m1,…,mr∈ℕ∗m_{1},\dots,m_{r}\in\mathbb{N}^{*}. There exists a diagram DD with the property: if ℒD​(m1,…,mr)\mathcal{L}_{D}(m_{1},\dots,m_{r}) is non-special then for all d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N} the system ℒd​(m1,…,mr)\mathcal{L}_{d}(m_{1},\dots,m_{r}) is non-special.

So for each rr such that ℒd​(m×r)∈S⁡(m,d0​(m))\mathcal{L}_{d}(m^{\times r})\in S(m,d_{0}(m)) we have to check only one system ℒD​(m×r)\mathcal{L}_{D}(m^{\times r}) for some diagram DD depending on rr. We also reduce this system to ℒD′​(m×9)\mathcal{L}_{D^{\prime}}(m^{\times 9}). In [6] the reader can find the table with the actual number of cases to be checked, as well as all necessary software with instructions, on how to perform the tests. ∎

Remark 33.

The test decribed above can also be performed for greater values of mm, but for each m≥43m\geq 43 this will take at least several days of computation. It seems that now it would be better to reorganize the method.

6. Closing remarks

Remark 34.

There exists another method of proving non-speciality of given system (or for a family of systems) based on blowing-up the projective space introduced by C. Ciliberto and R. Miranda ([5]). It seems that diagram cutting method is different and sometimes works better. Moreover, all definitions and results of section 3 can be easily carried over to the higher-dimensional case of the systems of polynomials in nn variables vanishing (with multiplicities) at points in general position. This is not known for the method of C. Ciliberto and R. Miranda.

Remark 35.

Observe that Theorem 27 can be reformulated to the following.

Theorem 36.

If the set EoLS⁡(m)\EoLS(m) contains only non-special systems and ℒd​(m1,…,mr)\mathcal{L}_{d}(m_{1},\dots,m_{r}) is non-special then

ℒd+m⁡(m+1)​(m1,…,mr,m×p)\mathcal{L}_{d+m(m+1)}(m_{1},\dots,m_{r},m^{\times p})

is non-special, where p=2​d+m⁡(m+1)+1p=2d+m(m+1)+1.

This shows that in order to find all non-special systems of the form ℒd​(m1,…,mr)\mathcal{L}_{d}(m_{1},\dots,m_{r}) with mi≤Mm_{i}\leq M, i=1,…,ri=1,\dots,r it is sufficient to check a finite number of cases.

Example 37.

We will show non-speciality of the system L=ℒ21​(7×6,6×4,1)L=\mathcal{L}_{21}(7^{\times 6},6^{\times 4},1) by diagram cutting method. The proof (found by a computer) can be easily read off from the picture. The system LL was studied in [10].
